card: The seat that does most to decide where the crisis goes. Will you write your ally a blank check?
intro: You are Wilhelm II, German Emperor and King of Prussia. Under the constitution you command the armed forces and hold the power to declare war, though a declaration of war needs the consent of the Federal Council (unless German territory has been attacked). Your empire of more than 65 million people raised its peacetime army to about 800,000 men under the Army Law of 1913, and the High Seas Fleet built up by Admiral Tirpitz is second only to Britain’s. Yet the largest party in the Reichstag is the Social Democrats, who have long opposed your military policy, and the only ally Germany can count on is Austria-Hungary. Beside you stand a cautious Chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, who fears Russia’s growing strength, and a chief of the General Staff, Moltke, who holds just one war plan, for the west, which strikes France first.

DE-00.place: Off Kiel, aboard the racing yacht Meteor
DE-00.title: News at Kiel Week

telegram.text: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Duchess of Hohenberg shot / Both dead / Assassin a young Bosnian Serb

DE-00.scene: On the afternoon of Sunday, 28 June, you are aboard your racing yacht Meteor for the Kiel Week regatta. A launch carrying Admiral von Müller, chief of the Naval Cabinet, comes alongside, and he calls across that the heir to the Austrian throne and his wife have been shot dead in Sarajevo. The British Second Battle Squadron lies in Kiel harbor on a goodwill visit for the regatta; a grand banquet at the castle was set for this afternoon, and the commander of the naval station is to give a dinner and ball tonight. Only two weeks ago the dead Archduke welcomed you as a friend at Konopiště, his estate in Bohemia.

voices.text: Your Majesty, you should return to Berlin at once and take this in hand yourself. The peace of Europe may turn on what Vienna does next, and at such a moment the German Emperor should not be seen lingering at a regatta.

voices.who: Prince Henry (the Kaiser’s brother, grand admiral)
voices.text: Your Majesty, the British squadron is here as our guest. If you break off Kiel Week and leave in a hurry, Europe will think Germany means to make a great affair of this. Send condolences, by all means, but let the program go on quietly.

choices.text: Take Prince Henry’s advice: let Kiel Week go on quietly and see the British squadron off, to show Germany will not inflame matters
choices.why: An emperor seen rushing about would only unsettle Europe
choices.after: The races went on, but the banquet and the ball were not held. London and Paris were relieved that the German Emperor had kept to his schedule, but Vienna noted that the sovereign of its closest ally had stayed on at the regatta.

choices.text: Break off Kiel Week to share your ally’s grief, return to Berlin next morning, and announce you will attend the funeral
choices.why: A grieving ally must see Germany at its side, and at once
choices.after: The castle banquet and the naval station ball were canceled, and only the races went on, quietly. Early on 29 June you boarded your train at Kiel in heavy silence. The Empress, who had driven over from Grünholz, was in mourning and meant to accompany you to the funeral in Vienna.

choices.text: On reaching Berlin, have the official press blame the Serbian government, so that Vienna hears Germany’s view first
choices.why: Firmness from the start will make Serbia, and Russia behind it, back down
choices.after: Berlin’s nationalist papers cheered the statement. The St Petersburg press accused Germany of branding Serbia the culprit before any investigation had reported, and the hard-liners in Vienna took heart from Berlin’s stance.

note.text: That afternoon the British ambassador, Goschen, heard the news with tears in his eyes and said he had known the Archduke well and valued him as a friend. Admiral Warrender of the British squadron confided to Hase, the German naval liaison officer, that the crime would bring war between Serbia and Austria, that if Russia were drawn in, Germany and France could not stand aside, and that it would end in a world war.

DE-00a.title: The Funeral in Vienna
DE-00a.event: On the afternoon of 1 July a telegram from the German consul general in Sarajevo reached the Foreign Office in Berlin. It reported that ten to twelve conspirators had been sent out from Belgrade separately and passed on a reliable local informant’s strong advice that the German Emperor should not go to Vienna. The court in Vienna, for its part, would prefer not to invite foreign sovereigns to the funeral.
DE-00a.scene: You had meant to go to Vienna with your brother, Prince Henry, and stand by your friend on his last journey. At first Vienna’s leaders, too, hoped the two emperors would meet at the funeral and talk over the Serbian question in person. In a memorandum to Franz Joseph on 1 July, the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, wrote that the German Emperor was biased in Serbia’s favor and would need to be won over. But the Foreign Ministry in Vienna does not want the Russian Tsar, the British King or the French President to come, and the court means to keep the funeral short and simple.

voices.text: Your Majesty, this journey to Vienna is not a necessity of state but a gesture of friendship beyond what protocol requires. The crime in Sarajevo seems to have a far-reaching conspiracy behind it, and one assassination tends to inspire others. I cannot take responsibility for exposing Your Majesty needlessly to danger on foreign soil.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), later, in his memoirs
voices.text: Later I heard that one of the reasons for this was consideration for my personal safety; to this I naturally would have paid no attention.

choices.text: Stay in Berlin and send Prince Henry to Vienna with your wreath and condolences, to hear what Vienna’s leaders want
choices.why: A middle course: avoid the danger, keep the courtesies owed an ally
choices.after: Prince Henry laid the German Emperor’s wreath before the coffins of the Archduke and his wife. Vienna’s ministers received him courteously, but they did not hear the one thing they wanted to hear: the German Emperor’s own mind.

choices.text: Refuse to look afraid: dismiss the consul’s warning, go to Vienna and discuss Serbia with Franz Joseph in person
choices.why: Only face to face with the old Emperor can you steer Vienna’s decision
choices.after: The court in Vienna was dismayed but could not stop the German Emperor from coming. On 3 July you arrived in Vienna under heavy guard and arranged to see the old Emperor privately after the funeral mass.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s advice and the consul’s warning, cancel the visit, and have it announced that you are unwell
choices.why: No occasion is urgent enough to stake the Emperor’s safety on it
choices.after: It was announced that the German Emperor had been taken ill, and the talk was of lumbago. When word followed that Prince Henry would not go either, rumors spread. At your wish Ambassador Tschirschky told Franz Joseph the true reason in person, and the old Emperor replied that he was, if anything, relieved the German Emperor was not coming.

note.text: The Archduke’s wife, Sophie, came from a Bohemian family of counts, so under Habsburg house law the marriage was morganatic, and she could not be laid in the imperial crypt of the Capuchin Church. The couple were buried together at Artstetten Castle, near the Danube.

map.caption: The Emperor back in Potsdam from Kiel on 29 June, while Vienna prepares the funeral of the Archduke and his wife

pressure.title: A Friend’s Funeral
pressure.text: You wanted to go to the funeral yourself, and the Empress, in mourning, prepared to go with you. In your memoirs you later wrote that you gave up the visit at Vienna’s request and heard only afterward that your personal safety had also been a concern, but the record of 2 July tells a different story. The Chancellor talked you out of the visit, citing the warning from the consul general in Sarajevo, and you wrote in your own hand that you feared it would look as if you were afraid, and had this passed on to Franz Joseph. Vienna’s leaders had wanted to win you over in person at the funeral; the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, thought you were biased in Serbia’s favor. If the visit is canceled, what the two emperors have to say to each other will travel by letter and envoy.

DE-00V.title: Two Emperors at the Hofburg
DE-00V.scene: After the funeral mass, the 83-year-old Emperor Franz Joseph receives you in his study at the Hofburg. Beside him stand his foreign minister, Berchtold, and the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza. Berchtold wants to settle the Serbian question once and for all; Tisza objects that a hasty attack could turn Romania into an enemy as well. The old Emperor says little and waits for your answer.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Belgrade is behind this crime. If we give way once more, the South Slavs inside the Monarchy will look to Belgrade alone. All we need is your assurance that Germany will stand beside us if Russia intervenes.

Your Majesty, if troops move before the Serbian government’s guilt has been shown, Europe will see Austria as the aggressor. We should first press Serbia through diplomacy and bring Bulgaria into the alliance, to change the balance of power in the Balkans.

choices.text: Grant Berchtold’s request on the spot, pledge Germany’s support, and urge haste before Europe’s sympathy cools
choices.why: Strike while sympathy lasts and the war will stay small
choices.after: Franz Joseph nodded, but he wanted the spoken promise confirmed in writing. Two days later Ambassador Szögyény came to the New Palace in Potsdam with the old Emperor’s handwritten letter.

choices.text: Advise as Tisza’s memorandum urged: diplomatic pressure first, and no troop movements until Belgrade’s guilt is shown
choices.why: An attack without proof would brand Austria the aggressor
choices.after: Tisza was relieved and Berchtold’s face hardened. Vienna dropped its plan to send an envoy to Berlin, and the hard-liners who had counted on unconditional German backing muttered that the German Emperor had pulled back at the decisive moment.

choices.text: Withhold a firm answer: the Chancellor must answer for any imperial pledge, so promise a written reply once you have consulted him
choices.why: A pledge from the Emperor alone cannot bind the German government
choices.after: Berchtold could not hide his disappointment. Vienna decided to ask for Germany’s position in an official document and entrusted the journey to Berlin to Count Hoyos, chef de cabinet to the foreign minister.

note.text: In fact the two emperors did not meet at the funeral. Franz Joseph’s letter dated 2 July and a memorandum on Balkan policy reached Potsdam on 5 July through Count Hoyos and Ambassador Szögyény. Franz Joseph signed the letter himself, but Hoyos had drafted it.

DE-01.title: The Blank Check

telegram.text: All ships flags at half-mast / Austrian flag at the mainmast / Heir to Austrian throne assassinated

DE-01.event: On 4 July Zimmermann, under secretary at the Foreign Office in Berlin, told Ambassador Szögyény that he sympathized with Vienna’s position, but warned against confronting Serbia with humiliating demands.
DE-01.scene: On Sunday, 5 July, the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Szögyény, comes to lunch at the New Palace and hands you a letter from Emperor Franz Joseph together with a memorandum on Balkan policy. Count Hoyos, chef de cabinet to Foreign Minister Berchtold, left Vienna last night to bring the papers. In the letter Austria makes plain its intention to punish Serbia and asks whether Germany will stand beside it if Russia intervenes. Only three weeks ago you were the Archduke’s guest at Konopiště Castle in Bohemia.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), in the margin of Ambassador Tschirschky’s report of 30 June
voices.text: Now or never. / Let Tschirschky be good enough to drop this nonsense! The Serbs must be disposed of, and that right soon!

voices.who: Tschirschky (German ambassador in Vienna), report to the Chancellor of 30 June
voices.text: In Vienna many voices call for settling accounts with the Serbs once and for all. I warn, calmly but firmly, against hasty steps. Vienna has not yet decided what it wants to gain, or what would come after.

Your Majesty, if Austria backs down once again, Germany loses its last ally. But if Russia intervenes, a Balkan quarrel becomes a continental war. If Vienna does move, it must act as quickly as possible and keep the war within the narrowest bounds.

choices.text: Counsel against hasty steps, as Tschirschky has done in Vienna, and reply that the Balkan question is for diplomacy alone
choices.why: Germany’s safety comes before the ally’s pride
choices.after: Count Hoyos went back to Vienna empty-handed. Without German backing Austria could not take on Russia alone, and Vienna’s hard-liners muttered that Berlin had abandoned its ally.

choices.text: Promise Germany’s unconditional support even if Russia intervenes, and urge Vienna to act fast
choices.why: Fail to hold Vienna now and Germany’s last ally is lost
choices.after: After lunch you promised Szögyény Germany’s full support, adding that Russia was in no way ready for war. Szögyény reported this to Vienna that night, and the next day Bethmann Hollweg confirmed it officially. Historians call it the "blank check."

choices.text: Promise support on conditions: no humiliating demands, as Zimmermann warned yesterday, and consult Germany before acting
choices.why: Keep the alliance, but do not leave the decision for war to Vienna
choices.after: Szögyény left the New Palace flustered. Now that Germany had attached conditions, even Vienna’s hard-liners, eager for immediate action, could no longer do as they pleased.

note.text: On 28 June the British Second Battle Squadron was at Kiel on a goodwill visit for Kiel Week (the Kiel Canal, its widening just completed, had reopened four days earlier). The British ambassador, Goschen, was staying aboard Admiral Warrender’s flagship, King George V, but when the news arrived he was on the Emperor’s yacht Hohenzollern. That afternoon the Emperor ordered all ships to lower their flags to half-mast and to hoist the Austrian flag at the mainmast.

pressure.title: A Friend’s Death and Saving Face
pressure.text: The murdered Franz Ferdinand was close to you. Only about two weeks before the assassination, on 12–13 June, you stayed with him at his estate of Konopiště in Bohemia. Ever since you backed down in the Moroccan crisis of 1911, nationalists at home have accused you of indecision. Back down again, and the same accusations will pour in.

DE-01a.place: New Palace, Potsdam; Kiel in the afternoon
DE-01a.title: Sailing as Planned
DE-01a.clock: The day after the pledge to Vienna
DE-01a.event: At 5 p.m. on 5 July you called Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg, Under Secretary Zimmermann, War Minister Falkenhayn, Lyncker, chief of the Military Cabinet, and your adjutant general, Plessen, to the New Palace and read them Vienna’s letter. Those present agreed that the sooner Austria moved the better, and that Russia, though Serbia’s friend, would in the end stay out.
DE-01a.scene: The next morning you prepare to leave on your Norwegian cruise. It is a summer voyage you have made almost every year, and the dates are widely known. The Chancellor says Europe will be reassured if the Emperor leaves as planned, but you are uneasy about what lies ahead and hesitate to leave the country. At yesterday’s meeting War Minister Falkenhayn asked whether any preparations should be made just in case, and you told him there was no need; you could still change that answer before you go.

voices.text: Your Majesty, if you called off a journey so widely known, the situation would look graver than it is, and the blame for a war might even fall on Your Majesty. All Europe is waiting for word that the German Emperor has set out as planned.
Your Majesty, if Russia steps in, every day counts. Before you leave, order at least a check of rail transport and ammunition.

voices.who: Capelle (deputy and acting state secretary of the Navy Office), recalling in 1919 a talk in the New Palace garden on the morning of 6 July
voices.text: He did not believe in serious warlike developments. According to his view, the Czar would not in this case place himself on the side of regicides. Besides that, Russia and France were not prepared for war.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s advice: sail as planned, let the army chiefs stay on leave, and order no special preparations
choices.why: Business as usual will keep Europe from scenting a crisis
choices.after: You did not change your answer to Falkenhayn. The army chiefs left on their planned leave, and you went to Kiel and boarded the Hohenzollern. At Kiel you told Gustav Krupp von Bohlen, head of the Krupp firm, again and again that this time you would not back down, and Krupp is said to have found the display rather pitiful.

choices.text: Before leaving, telegraph Nicky that no monarch can side with regicides, and sound out whether Russia will shield Serbia
choices.why: Solidarity among monarchs may hold Russia back
choices.after: Nicholas II sent a courteous reply condemning the crime but said little about holding the Serbian government responsible. Vienna grew nervous at the thought of the German Emperor talking privately with the Tsar.

choices.text: Sail on the cruise, but first order Falkenhayn to check rail transport and ammunition stocks quietly
choices.why: If Russia steps in, the side that is a day ahead will win
choices.after: Falkenhayn quietly began checking rail transport and ammunition stocks. But the foreign military attachés in Berlin missed little, and reports that the German army was up to something began to reach Paris and St Petersburg.

note.text: Nicholas II’s grandfather, Alexander II, was killed by revolutionaries' bombs in St Petersburg in 1881. Some historians read Wilhelm’s belief that the Tsar would not side with "regicides" as resting on this sense of solidarity among monarchs.

DE-02.place: Off Balholm, Sognefjord, Norway, aboard the imperial yacht Hohenzollern
DE-02.title: Vienna Hesitates
DE-02.clock: Nine days until the ultimatum is delivered (6 p.m., 23 July)

telegram.text: Tisza now holds war unavoidable / Ultimatum text to be settled on 19th / Delivery after French President leaves St Petersburg (due 25th)

DE-02.event: Berlin’s leading figures have gone on their scheduled holidays so as not to arouse suspicion. Moltke, chief of the General Staff, is taking the cure at the Bohemian spa of Karlsbad, and Admiral Tirpitz, state secretary of the Navy Office, is at Tarasp in Switzerland.
DE-02.scene: You sailed from Kiel on 6 July, as planned, on your regular Norwegian cruise. The summer sun over the fjords stays up late into the night, but the telegrams from Berlin say only that Vienna has not yet moved. Tisza, the Hungarian prime minister, had opposed hasty military action, and many Austrian soldiers are on harvest leave and will not rejoin their units until around 25 July. The Foreign Office in Berlin has not yet seen the text of the ultimatum Vienna means to send.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Europe’s sympathy over Sarajevo cools with every passing day. Only if Vienna presents a fait accompli quickly can the conflict be confined to Serbia. You must urge Vienna on.

Your Majesty, British opinion is outraged by the crime in Sarajevo, but it will not go so far as to back the crushing of Serbia. If Austria goes too far, Russia will move, and if Russia and France move, Britain will not stand aside in the end.

voices.who: Bethmann Hollweg (Chancellor), to his secretary Riezler on the veranda at Hohenfinow on the night of 7 July (from Riezler’s diary, whose authenticity is disputed)
voices.text: The old dilemma at every Austrian action in the Balkans. If we encourage them, they say we pushed them into it. If we discourage them, they say we left them in the lurch. … The future belongs to Russia which grows and grows, looming above us as an increasingly terrifying nightmare.

choices.text: Heed Lichnowsky: obtain the ultimatum’s text in advance and have it toned down to terms Serbia could accept
choices.why: Lower demands are the price of not making Britain an enemy
choices.after: Berchtold was displeased but cut the harshest clauses from the text. At 6 p.m. on 23 July a softened note was delivered in Belgrade.

choices.text: Take Jagow’s line: press Vienna to act before Europe’s sympathy cools, but leave the wording of the ultimatum wholly to Vienna
choices.why: Only a quick fait accompli will keep the conflict contained
choices.after: The Foreign Office saw the text only on the evening of 22 July, the day before it went out, and the note delivered in Belgrade at 6 p.m. on 23 July was designed from the start to be rejected. On the 25th, minutes before the deadline, Serbia accepted most of it, with reservations on several points, but rejected point 6, which demanded that Austrian officials take part in the investigation. The Austrian minister, Giesl, left Belgrade on the 6:30 p.m. train that day.

note.text: According to Riezler’s diary entry of 14 July, Bethmann Hollweg called this policy "a leap in the dark and as such the most serious duty." But no original of the diary survives for the July crisis, only a version reworked later. The historian Bernd Sösemann questioned the authenticity and editing of this section, and its editor, Karl Dietrich Erdmann, rebutted him, so how far the wording can be trusted remains disputed.

DE-02B.place: Off Balholm, Norway, aboard the imperial yacht Hohenzollern
DE-02B.title: Vienna Pushes Back
DE-02B.clock: About 15 days until Austria’s soldiers return from harvest leave (around 25 July)

telegram.text: Foreign Minister Berchtold protests / Action impossible on German conditions / Monarchy’s standing in Balkans finished

DE-02B.scene: When word came that Germany had attached conditions, the Foreign Ministry on Vienna’s Ballhausplatz was in uproar. Foreign Minister Berchtold protests sharply through Ambassador Szögyény, and Conrad, the chief of the General Staff, has begun to say that Germany is an ally who cannot be trusted. Over the past few years Conrad has called for a preventive war against Serbia dozens of times. On your yacht at anchor in the fjord, you must decide whether to hold firm or give way.

voices.text: Your Majesty, with German conditions attached, Vienna can do nothing. If the Monarchy gives way once more, it is finished in the Balkans, and the South Slavs within it will look only to Belgrade and St Petersburg.

Your Majesty, if you withdraw the conditions, Germany will share the responsibility for whatever Vienna writes. But if you insist on them, Vienna will take it that Germany has abandoned the alliance. Either way there is a price.

choices.text: Have the Chancellor tell Szögyény again, plainly, that Germany will back only demands Serbia could accept
choices.why: Demands that widen the war must be blocked, whatever Vienna says
choices.after: Vienna swallowed its displeasure and revised the text. Conrad complained to his circle that Germany had tied Austria hand and foot.

choices.text: Accept Szögyény’s protest, withdraw the conditions, and say again that Germany will back whatever means Vienna chooses
choices.why: Losing the ally’s trust would cost more than the risk of war
choices.after: Vienna was relieved, and the ultimatum’s wording grew harsh again. Delivered at 6 p.m. on 23 July, it was largely accepted by Serbia on the 25th except for point 6, and the Austrian minister, Giesl, left Belgrade at once.

note.text: In the summer of 1914 many soldiers of the Austro-Hungarian army were on leave to bring in the harvest and were not due back with their units until around 25 July. This is why Vienna could not take military action straight away in early July.

DE-02a.place: Off Balholm, Sognefjord, Norway, aboard the imperial yacht Hohenzollern
DE-02a.title: Recall the Fleet?
DE-02a.clock: A few hours before the deadline for Serbia’s reply (6 p.m., Belgrade time)

telegram.from: Belgrade (Minister Griesinger), relayed by the Foreign Office in Berlin
telegram.text: Serbian military firmly demands rejection of ultimatum and war / Mobilization already well under way

DE-02a.scene: At 9:30 this morning, after reading a telegram from the Wolff news agency, you ordered the fleet to hurry its coaling and be ready to sail at any moment. No separate report on the situation has come from the Foreign Office in Berlin; you learned the terms of the ultimatum from the press bulletins sent out by the Norddeich radio station. On 19 July you ordered the High Seas Fleet to be kept together until the 25th so that it could break off the cruise and return at any time, but on the 22nd the Chancellor and the Foreign Office arranged for it to stay on in Norway as planned. The Admiralty Staff has reported that if Britain declares war, the British fleet will certainly launch a surprise attack on the German fleet. As far as you know, Russian torpedo boat flotillas are exercising in the Baltic, and there is not a single German battleship in those waters.

voices.who: Bethmann Hollweg (Chancellor), telegram of 23 July to Count Wedel in the Emperor’s suite (written by Jagow in the Chancellor’s name)
voices.text: Any premature recall of our Fleet might cause general uneasiness and be regarded as suspicious, especially in England.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), in the margin of the Chancellor’s telegram of 25 July urging delay of the fleet’s return (received on the voyage home, morning of the 26th)
voices.text: When Russia mobilizes my fleet must be already in the Baltic, so it is going home.

choices.text: Overrule the Chancellor and head home, ordering the High Seas Fleet back as well, since the Baltic cannot be left empty
choices.why: The fleet’s safety comes before a civilian Chancellor’s worries
choices.after: That afternoon you ordered the fleet to assemble and sail for home as soon as it had finished coaling, and you too left Balholm. In the margin of the Chancellor’s telegram, received on the way home on the morning of the 26th, you wrote that military measures were decided not on the strength of a news agency report but on that of the general situation, which the "civilian" Chancellor had not yet grasped. When a second request from the Chancellor to keep the fleet in Norway arrived on the morning of the 27th, you wrote in the margin: "There is a Russian fleet! … Port Arthur should be a lesson! My Fleet has orders to sail for Kiel, and to Kiel it is going to sail!"

choices.text: Return home yourself, but heed the Chancellor’s warning not to provoke Britain: leave the High Seas Fleet in Norway a while longer
choices.why: A hurried recall of the fleet would make Britain suspect Germany
choices.after: Hearing that the fleet had stayed in the fjords, the Admiralty in London concluded that Germany was not yet in a hurry. But the Admiralty Staff in Berlin grew more anxious by the day, with no battleships to guard the entrance to the Baltic.

note.text: In February 1904 the Japanese navy attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur (Lüshun) with torpedo boats before declaring war. The "lesson of Port Arthur" Wilhelm had in mind was the fear that the fleet might be attacked before war was declared, or be cut off from home if the Danish Belts were closed.

map.caption: Kiel, where the High Seas Fleet would return; Kronstadt, base of Russia’s Baltic Fleet; and Portland, where Britain’s main fleet lay

pressure.title: A "Civilian" Chancellor and a News Agency Wire
pressure.text: On 25 July you learned of events not from the Foreign Office in Berlin but from a news agency telegram. In your memoirs you wrote that while at Balholm you received only meager news from the Foreign Office and had to rely on the Norwegian newspapers, and that you said several times you would return home but were told each time to continue your journey. In the margin of the Chancellor’s telegram you underlined the word "civilian" and wrote that the Chancellor did not understand the situation. If you follow the Chancellor’s advice, it may look to the navy and your entourage as if the Emperor is being led by a civilian official.

DE-03M.place: North Sea, the Hohenzollern on her way home
DE-03M.title: Serbia Accepts Everything
DE-03M.clock: Just after the ultimatum expired (6 p.m., 25 July)

telegram.text: Serbian reply / All points accepted / Participation of Austrian officials in inquiry also accepted

DE-03M.scene: Faced with the softened note, Serbia accepted every point just before the deadline. Vienna has lost its pretext for military action, but Conrad is furious: Serbia’s promises are empty words, he says, and it must be attacked all the same. On the yacht heading home, a telegram arrives from Vienna asking what Germany wants.

voices.who: Conrad (Austro-Hungarian chief of the General Staff), as relayed from Vienna
voices.text: Serbia’s promises cannot be trusted. Unless the army goes into Belgrade and takes guarantees, the same thing will happen again in two years.

Your Majesty, we have won a diplomatic victory without shedding a drop of blood. Neither Russia nor France has any grounds to object. If we stop here and hold on to this victory, we may even shake the unity of the Triple Entente.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s view: urge Vienna to rest content with a bloodless diplomatic victory, and refuse to back military action
choices.why: Securing a game already won is the greater victory
choices.after: Vienna seemed to agree, reluctantly, but the hard-liners at the Foreign Ministry and Conrad, insisting that Serbia’s promises could not be trusted, kept their mobilization preparations in place. In London, Grey began to plan a conference to settle the affair.

choices.text: Accept Conrad’s view that Serbia’s promises are worthless, and reply that you will not stand in the way if Vienna wants to act
choices.why: Germany cannot block what its ally is set on doing
choices.after: Vienna declared Serbia’s reply insincere and broke off relations. As news spread that Austria meant to attack a country that had accepted every demand, European opinion quickly turned against it.

note.text: In fact Serbia rejected point 6, under which Austrian officials would take part in a judicial inquiry inside Serbia, as a violation of its sovereignty. That single point became the immediate reason for the break in relations.

DE-03.title: Grey Proposes a Four-Power Conference
DE-03.clock: Two days after Austria broke off relations with Serbia

telegram.text: Grey proposal / Conference in London of British, German, French, Italian ambassadors / All military operations to be suspended meanwhile

DE-03.event: Having landed at Kiel on 27 July, you receive Bethmann Hollweg’s report at Potsdam that afternoon.
DE-03.scene: Bethmann Hollweg reports a proposal from the British foreign secretary, Sir Edward Grey: the ambassadors of the four powers without a direct stake, Britain, Germany, France and Italy, should meet in London to find a solution, and all military operations should stop in the meantime. During the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913, too, a conference of ambassadors in London helped keep the great powers out of war. But if Germany agrees, Austria will have to submit its quarrel with Serbia to the judgment of the European powers.

voices.text: Your Majesty, agreeing to a conference would mean putting Austria before a European court of arbitration. Our ally would never accept such a humiliation. Direct talks between Vienna and St Petersburg would be better.
Your Majesty, Grey’s proposal is the last chance for Britain and Germany to keep the peace together. If we reject it, London will conclude that Germany wants war.

choices.text: Follow Lichnowsky: accept the ambassadors' conference in London and defend Austria’s interests there, as in 1913
choices.why: Only by working with Britain can a continental war be avoided
choices.after: Austria was unhappy, but without Germany it could not refuse the conference. In London, preparations began for the four ambassadors to meet.

choices.text: Follow Jagow: decline the conference and urge Vienna and St Petersburg to settle the Austro-Serbian dispute in direct talks
choices.why: An ally cannot be put on trial before the great powers
choices.after: On 27 July Germany declined the proposed conference and recommended direct talks between Vienna and St Petersburg. At the Foreign Office in London, suspicion grew that Germany wanted war.

note.text: The conference was the idea of Sir Arthur Nicolson, permanent under secretary at the Foreign Office; Grey adopted it and sent it to the powers on 26 July. The London Conference of Ambassadors, held from December 1912 to August 1913, settled Albania’s independence and kept the Balkan Wars from spreading into a war between the great powers.

DE-04.title: Every Reason for War Drops Away
DE-04.clock: About an hour until Vienna telegraphs its declaration of war
DE-04.event: At around 11 a.m. Vienna, calling Serbia’s reply untrustworthy, will telegraph its declaration of war. You do not yet know this.
DE-04.scene: On the morning after your return from Norway, you read a copy of Serbia’s reply for the first time, and as your pen moves along the margin an idea comes to you. The Austrian army would occupy Belgrade alone, as a pledge, and halt there to see whether Serbia keeps its promises. The question now is how, and how forcefully, to put this to Vienna.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), in the margin of a copy of Serbia’s reply
voices.text: A brilliant performance for a time-limit of only forty-eight hours. This is more than one could have expected! A great moral victory for Vienna; but with it every reason for war drops away, and Giesl might have remained quietly in Belgrade!
Your Majesty, Grey believes Serbia’s reply can serve as a basis for negotiation. If Berlin does not move Vienna, Britain will come to believe that Germany wants this war.
Your Majesty, Russia has already begun military preparations on its borders. Germany cannot be the only one sitting idle while the diplomats trade words.

choices.text: Bypass the Chancellor and wire Franz Joseph directly: stop once Belgrade is taken and negotiate, or there will be no support
choices.why: Only a message from the Emperor himself will not be watered down
choices.after: The 83-year-old Emperor was shaken, but he knew he could not face Russia without Germany. Vienna reluctantly replied that it would stop at Belgrade.

choices.text: Agree with Falkenhayn that this is no time to sit idle: back the declaration of war and press Vienna to finish Serbia fast
choices.why: A quick war leaves Russia no opening to step in
choices.after: Around 2 a.m. on 29 July, Austrian river monitors and the batteries at Zemun (Semlin), across the Sava, opened fire on Belgrade. The Serbian capital stood right on the river that formed the border.

choices.text: Send the "halt in Belgrade" plan to Jagow in a handwritten letter, for the Foreign Office to pass on to Vienna
choices.why: Letting the ally save face may be the way to stop the war
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg passed your plan to Vienna only at 10:15 that night, telling the ambassador to "avoid very carefully giving rise to the impression that we wish to hold Austria back," and he left out your words that "every reason for war drops away." By then Vienna had already declared war, and it all but ignored the advice.

note.text: Wilhelm’s "halt in Belgrade" idea was almost the same as the mediation proposal that the British foreign secretary, Grey, put to Lichnowsky the next day. Berlin and London had arrived at the same solution, but little time was left to move Vienna.

map.caption: Belgrade, a border city facing Zemun (Semlin) across the Sava

pressure.title: Orders Pass Through Other Hands
pressure.text: The Emperor’s wishes do not reach Vienna unaltered. Your letters cross the desks of the Foreign Office and the Chancellor before becoming telegrams, and along the way sentences may be changed or dispatch delayed. Even during the Norwegian cruise, the reports you received were the ones Berlin chose to send.

DE-05.title: Willy and Nicky
DE-05.clock: The day Russia announces partial mobilization

telegram.text: An ignoble war has been declared to a weak country / I foresee that very soon I shall be overwhelmed by the pressure brought upon me and be forced to take extreme measures which will lead to war / To try and avoid such a calamity as a European war I beg you in the name of our old friendship / to do what you can to stop your allies from going too far / Nicky

DE-05.event: On 29 July Russia announced partial mobilization in the four military districts nearest the Austrian border: Odessa, Kiev, Moscow and Kazan. Since the early hours of the same day the Austrian army has been shelling Belgrade.
DE-05.scene: For years you and the Russian Emperor, Nicholas II, have called each other "Willy" and "Nicky" in your telegrams and letters, which are written in English. You are distant relatives, and Nicholas’s wife, Empress Alexandra, is your first cousin. The same Nicky with whom you sealed your friendship at Baltic Port in 1912 has now ordered mobilization. In the afternoon the Chancellor, the chief of the General Staff and the war minister gather at the New Palace to decide how to answer Russia’s partial mobilization.

voices.who: Moltke (chief of the General Staff), memorandum to the Chancellor of this day
voices.text: After this fashion things must and will develop, unless, one might say, a miracle happens to prevent at the last moment a war which will annihilate for decades the civilization of almost all Europe.

Your Majesty, Russia must order general mobilization first, so that Germany is the side defending itself. Only then will the Social Democrats' workers follow, seeing it as a war against the Tsar’s Russia. If Germany moves first, we lose everything.

choices.text: Appeal to Nicky in a personal telegram, while having Ambassador Pourtalès warn that if Russia goes on mobilizing, Germany will too
choices.why: A warm appeal and a clear warning together may stop the Tsar
choices.after: At 6:30 p.m. you telegraphed that Russian military measures would "jeopardize my position as mediator which I readily accepted on your appeal to my friendship and my help," and that night Nicholas II turned the general mobilization order he had already signed back into a partial one. But that same night Nicky asked you to explain why your friendly telegram and your ambassador’s warning did not match, and the reprieve lasted barely a day.

choices.text: Russia has moved first: proclaim the "state of imminent danger of war" at once, as Moltke urged in today’s memorandum
choices.why: Each day’s delay in mobilizing lowers the odds of victory
choices.after: The streets of Berlin began to stir. The Russian General Staff pressed the Tsar, pointing out that Germany had moved first, and the Social Democratic press accused the government of rushing into war.

choices.text: Leave out the ambassador’s warning and send only a warm personal telegram, giving Nicky room to curb his generals
choices.why: Without a threat, the Tsar can keep his hard-liners in check
choices.after: Nicholas II was relieved by a telegram that carried no warning. Whether the Russian army stops at partial mobilization will depend on how far Vienna gives way.

note.text: That night Nicholas II telegraphed again, proposing that the Austro-Serbian problem be referred to the Hague conference, but you did not answer the proposal in your next telegram. When the German Foreign Office published the two emperors' telegrams during the war, this one was left out.

DE-06.title: Can Britain’s Neutrality Be Bought?

telegram.text: Grey warns / If conflict stays between Austria and Russia, Britain can stand aside / If Germany and France drawn in, Britain cannot stand by

DE-06.scene: Bethmann Hollweg means to summon the British ambassador, Goschen, and offer a bargain: if Britain stays neutral, Germany, even if victorious, will take no territory from metropolitan France. He makes no promise about France’s colonies, and of Belgium he says only that, if it does not fight Germany, its territory will be left intact after the war. In effect he is signaling that Germany intends to march through Belgium. Belgian neutrality was guaranteed jointly by Britain, France, Austria, Russia and Prussia in the Treaty of London of 1839, and Germany inherited Prussia’s obligations.

voices.text: Your Majesty, if only Britain stands aside, this war will be settled on the Continent. What King George V told Prince Henry, too, meant that Britain wishes to remain neutral.
Your Majesty, a king’s words are not a promise from the British cabinet. Britain will never simply watch France collapse, and the German fleet is not yet ready to take on the British fleet.
Your Majesty, Germany has only one plan for the west, and its road runs through Belgium. The great eastern deployment plan, for a war against Russia alone, has not been updated since 1913.

choices.text: Offer nothing, since a rash offer would only betray the march through Belgium, and watch which way the British cabinet leans
choices.why: Better to wait for London’s decision than to show your hand early
choices.after: London puzzled over Germany’s silence. Most of the Liberal cabinet was still against going to war.

choices.text: Pledge to respect Belgian neutrality, even if it delays Moltke’s plan, so that Britain has no cause to join the war
choices.why: Keeping Britain out matters more than the war plan
choices.after: Grey welcomed it, but Moltke protested fiercely that the promise blocked the German army’s only war plan. Before long you will have to decide again whether to keep it or break it.

choices.text: Summon Ambassador Goschen and promise that if Britain stays neutral, Germany will claim no land in metropolitan France
choices.why: If France proper is left untouched, Britain may stand aside
choices.after: On receiving Goschen’s report, Grey firmly rejected the offer the next day. To strike such a bargain at France’s expense, he said, would be a disgrace from which Britain’s good name would never recover.

note.text: Meeting Prince Henry on 26 July, George V said he hoped Britain would stay neutral, but also that he feared Britain would be drawn in if Germany fought Russia and France joined. Wilhelm took this as a promise of British neutrality. When Tirpitz voiced doubts at Potsdam on 29 July, Wilhelm replied, as Tirpitz recorded in his memoirs, "I have the word of a king, and that is sufficient for me."

pressure.title: A King’s Word
pressure.text: On 26 July King George V told your brother, Prince Henry, who was visiting London, that Britain would try to keep out of this and remain neutral. The King’s own record adds that he feared Britain would be drawn in if Germany fought Russia and France joined. Even so, you took his words as a promise that Britain would stay neutral. When Tirpitz had doubts, you replied that you had the King’s word and that was enough.

DE-07.place: New Palace, Potsdam; the Berlin Palace in the afternoon
DE-07.title: Russia Mobilizes
DE-07.clock: First day of Russia’s general mobilization

telegram.text: General mobilization of Russian army and navy ordered / First mobilization day 31 July

DE-07.event: Russia has begun general mobilization, which means moving not only the troops on the Austrian border but also those facing Germany.
DE-07.scene: Moltke says every day’s delay reduces Germany’s chances. The German war plan stakes everything on defeating France in the west before Russia can complete its mobilization. Yesterday you poured out your fury in the margin of a report, writing that Britain, Russia and France had conspired to encircle Germany. In the Lustgarten in front of the Berlin Palace, crowds are gathering to wait for news.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Russia’s mobilization has begun. Every day Germany waits puts East Prussia in greater danger and shortens the time to finish France in the west. You must decide now.

Your Majesty, before any declaration of war, Russia must be given one last chance to answer. Only then will the world see clearly that it was Russia that started the war. Mobilization means war, so the steps must be taken in the right order.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), in the margin of a report, around 30 July
voices.text: Edward VII is stronger after his death than am I who am still alive!

choices.text: Hold back mobilization and wire Nicky and George V directly: one last try for a compromise, with Vienna halting at Belgrade
choices.why: A last exchange between sovereigns is worth more than mobilization
choices.after: Berlin’s generals and the right-wing press accused the Emperor of losing his nerve. And Russia’s mobilization advanced day by day.

choices.text: Proclaim the "state of imminent danger of war," demand Russia halt mobilization within 12 hours, and ask France to stay neutral
choices.why: Russia mobilized first, so Germany is the one defending itself
choices.after: A secret instruction went with the demand to France: if France chose neutrality, it was to hand over its border fortresses of Toul and Verdun as a pledge. But France replied only that it "would act in accordance with her interests," so this demand was never presented. Russia did not reply. That evening, from the palace balcony, you told the crowd that "envious peoples everywhere are compelling us to our just defense."

choices.text: Order mobilization, but take Russia at its word that mobilization is not war: defer a declaration and keep negotiating
choices.why: Get the army ready without closing the door on diplomacy
choices.after: Moltke repeated that for Germany mobilization meant an advance. The brigades due to assemble near Aachen by the third day of mobilization and take Liège in Belgium by surprise were already preparing to move.

note.text: Nicholas II, who had canceled general mobilization on the night of 29 July, approved it again on the afternoon of 30 July after Foreign Minister Sazonov persuaded him. The German government, for its part, had already decided not to arrest the Social Democratic leaders if war came.

pressure.title: Encirclement, and Time Running Out
pressure.text: On 30 July you wrote a long, furious note in the margin of a report: Britain, Russia and France had long conspired to encircle Germany, and the encirclement was at last complete. Moltke says every day’s delay reduces Germany’s chances. If you put off mobilization, the anger of the army and the right-wing press will turn on you.

DE-08.title: Lichnowsky’s Telegram
DE-08.clock: About two hours until the planned entry into Luxembourg (7 p.m.)

telegram.text: Grey on telephone / Asks whether, if France remains neutral in a Russo-German war, Germany would undertake not to attack France / I assured him I could take responsibility for such a guaranty

DE-08.event: You have just signed the order for general mobilization, at 5 p.m. This evening in St Petersburg, Ambassador Pourtalès will hand Sazonov the declaration of war.
DE-08.scene: Moltke is leaving the palace after the signing when he is called back: a telegram has come from Lichnowsky in London. When you exclaim, elated, "Then we simply deploy the whole army in the east!" Moltke’s face sets hard. His uncle was the elder Moltke, who led Prussia to victory in the wars of German unification.

voices.who: Moltke (chief of the General Staff), as reported in his memoirs
voices.text: Your Majesty, that cannot be done. The deployment of an army of millions cannot be improvised. Overturn a year’s work, and all that is left is a confused mass of armed men without supplies.
Your uncle would have given me a different answer!

voices.who: Bethmann Hollweg (Chancellor) and Jagow (state secretary, Foreign Office)
voices.text: Your Majesty, if the neutrality of both Britain and France can be had, we must not let this telegram slip. At the very least, the advance in the west must stop until Britain confirms it officially.

choices.text: Follow the Chancellor and Jagow: halt the advance into Luxembourg and the west until Britain confirms it officially
choices.why: Little is lost by waiting until confirmation arrives
choices.realNote: Wilhelm did halt the entry for a time, then, after receiving George V’s telegram that night, let Moltke’s plan go ahead. In the meantime, around 7 p.m., an advance party of the 69th Infantry Regiment entered the station at Troisvierges (Ulflingen) in Luxembourg, then withdrew on receiving the halt order.
choices.after: You ordered the entry into Luxembourg stopped. Moltke refused to sign the halt order and wrote in his memoirs that on returning home he "wept tears of despair like a broken man." Around 11 p.m., when George V’s telegram revealed the misunderstanding, you summoned Moltke and told him, "Now you can do what you like."

choices.text: Accept Moltke’s point that the telegram is unconfirmed, and let the entry into Luxembourg go ahead at 7 p.m. as planned
choices.why: A year’s planning cannot be overturned on the strength of one telegram
choices.after: Moltke withdrew, looking relieved. In 1914 Wilhelm did not follow Moltke at once but halted the entry into Luxembourg for a time. Either way, George V’s telegram that night revealed that Lichnowsky’s report rested on a misunderstanding.

choices.text: Overrule Moltke and, by imperial authority, deploy the whole army in the east, standing on the defensive in the west
choices.why: Here is the chance to fight Russia alone, without Britain and France
choices.after: Moltke protested strongly but obeyed. Redrawing the railway timetables delayed the eastern deployment by nearly two weeks.

note.text: Moltke had stopped updating the great eastern deployment plan in 1913, so in 1914 Germany had only the western plan. After the war Staab, head of the General Staff’s railway section, claimed that four of the seven armies could have been sent east by 15 August, but this claim is disputed.

map.caption: Troisvierges, at Luxembourg’s northern tip, which a German advance party entered and left on the evening of 1 August

DE-09a.title: Italy Stays Neutral
DE-09a.clock: Second day of the war with Russia

telegram.text: Cabinet decided yesterday no alliance obligation / Austria’s war one of aggression, Italy not consulted beforehand / Neutral for now, leaving room to join allies later

DE-09a.event: Today in Constantinople, Ambassador Wangenheim and the Ottoman grand vizier, Said Halim, signed a secret treaty of alliance. If Russia intervened with military action and Germany had to come to Austria’s aid, the Ottoman Empire would take on the same obligation. The treaty followed your instruction of 24 July, given over Wangenheim’s objections, to accept Enver’s offer of an alliance.
DE-09a.scene: Italy, a member of the Triple Alliance since 1882, has chosen neutrality. Rome argues that Austria did not consult it before sending the ultimatum, and that a war against Serbia is not a defensive war. Under Article 7 of the alliance treaty, if Austria changes the status quo in the Balkans it must first agree on compensation with Italy, and the compensation Rome wants is the Trentino, which is Austrian territory. On 27 July you gave explicit orders that Vienna be told to settle Article 7 and compensation with Italy in good time, but Vienna did nothing.

voices.who: Wilhelm II (you), in the margin of Flotow’s report from Rome of 24 July (forwarded by Jagow on the 25th)
voices.text: The little thief must always have his swallow, too. / That is all bosh and it will come out all right in the end of itself, in the course of events.

Your Majesty, Italy must be held in the Triple Alliance at all costs. If Italy threatens Austria from behind, the Austrian army cannot throw its full strength against Russia, so you must press Vienna hard to promise compensation.

Your Majesty, Italy’s neutrality is a disappointment, but it is better than having Italy as an enemy. Pressing Rome hard will only push it toward the Triple Entente; we should work to keep its neutrality benevolent.

choices.text: Publicly demand that Rome honor its alliance duty, and warn that betrayal has a price, so that Romania does not follow
choices.why: Let one ally break its word and the whole alliance wavers
choices.after: When Berlin’s warning appeared in the Roman papers, Italian opinion turned against Austria and Germany instead. The Salandra government did not abandon neutrality, and the Entente ambassadors began calling on the Italian foreign minister more often.

choices.text: Do as Moltke asks: wire Franz Joseph directly and press him to hold Italy even at the cost of giving up the Trentino
choices.why: A safe southern front is worth more than the Trentino
choices.after: The telegram went to Vienna that night. No one can say how the old Emperor will answer an ally’s demand that he give up long-held lands of his empire.

choices.text: Take Jagow’s advice: accept Italy’s neutrality so it does not become an enemy, and keep pressing Vienna to negotiate compensation
choices.why: A neutral Italy is better than a hostile one
choices.after: Germany kept up relations with Italy and repeatedly urged Vienna to negotiate compensation, but for a long time Vienna refused to give up the Trentino. In December 1914 Germany sent the former chancellor Bülow to the Rome embassy to carry on the negotiations, but in April 1915 Italy joined the Entente under the Treaty of London and on 23 May declared war on Austria-Hungary.

note.text: Jagow, state secretary at the Foreign Office, had been ambassador in Rome from 1909 to January 1913. The Austrian territories of the Trentino and Trieste had many Italian-speaking inhabitants, so relations between Vienna and Rome stayed uneasy even after they became allies.

map.caption: Rome, which announced its neutrality on 2 August, and Constantinople, which signed a secret alliance with Germany the same day

DE-09I.title: The Price of the Trentino

telegram.text: Emperor Franz Joseph’s answer / Immediate cession of Trentino impossible / Willing to discuss compensation after the war

DE-09I.scene: Vienna’s answer has come tonight, sooner than expected. The old Emperor says he cannot give up long-held lands of his empire under pressure from an ally, but that compensation can be discussed once the war is over. What Rome wants is not a promise but an actual handover. For a Germany now at war with Russia, which side its southern ally takes is no small matter.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Vienna is furious that Germany is using an ally’s territory as a bargaining chip. Press any harder and the bond between Emperor Franz Joseph and Your Majesty will be damaged beyond repair.
Your Majesty, as long as Italy threatens Austria from behind, the Austrian army cannot throw its full weight against Russia. If the Trentino alone can remove that danger, it is not a high price.

choices.text: Heed Tschirschky’s warning: accept Vienna’s answer, and at least have a written promise of postwar compensation sent to Rome
choices.why: Keeping faith with the ally matters more than Italy
choices.after: Rome received the document but shook its head. In Rome’s view a postwar promise would mean whatever the victor chose, and Italy stayed neutral, weighing the offers of both sides.

choices.text: Take Moltke’s view that the Trentino is a fair price: press Vienna, threatening to cut German help in the east if it refuses
choices.why: Italy must be held, even at the cost of bruising the ally
choices.after: Franz Joseph was enraged, but he knew he could not face Russia without Germany. Vienna agreed in principle to cede the Trentino, and Rome, while staying neutral, promised not to attack Austria. At the Viennese court a deep resentment remained that Berlin had sold off an ally’s land.

note.text: On 15 July Jagow did write to Tschirschky that the only compensation that would satisfy Italy was the Trentino, while acknowledging that giving up long-held territory would be very hard for the Austrian Emperor and people to accept. On 20 July Berchtold brushed the advice aside, saying compensation was not yet a live question.

DE-09.title: The Road Through Belgium
DE-09.clock: Demand for passage delivered to Belgium (7 p.m.) / 12 hours to reply

telegram.from: Foreign Office, Berlin → Legation in Brussels
telegram.text: Open sealed envelope at once / Deliver to Belgian government by 8 p.m. today / 12 hours for reply

DE-09.event: This morning German troops entered Luxembourg. The railways across the Grand Duchy are a vital supply route for the advance in the west.
DE-09.scene: Under the western war plan, Belgium comes next. At the German legation in Brussels lies a sealed envelope, brought by special courier on 29 July: a note demanding that Belgium allow German troops to pass. Going through Belgium would outflank France’s line of border fortresses, but it would give Britain, a guarantor of Belgian neutrality, a reason to enter the war.

voices.text: Your Majesty, unless the twelve forts of Liège are taken in the first days of mobilization, the western campaign stalls at the outset. Krupp’s 42-centimeter mortars will break the forts, and if Belgium opens the road, no blood need be shed.

Your Majesty, the moment Belgian neutrality is trampled, the noninterventionists in the British cabinet will have no ground left to stand on. Only if Belgium is left alone will Britain stay on its own side of the water.

choices.text: Have the legation in Brussels deliver the note held there, demanding that Belgium let German troops pass within 12 hours
choices.why: A quick fall of Liège matters more than Britain’s anger
choices.after: At 7 a.m. on 3 August the Belgian government, meeting under King Albert I, rejected the demand. That evening Germany declared war on France, citing the baseless claim that French aircraft had bombed the area near Nuremberg, and on the morning of 4 August German troops crossed the Belgian border.

choices.text: Stand on the defensive in the west and wait, since Britain will have no cause to step in unless France attacks first
choices.why: The side that does not strike first has the stronger case abroad
choices.after: Moltke offered to resign, and the German papers wrote that the Emperor could not make up his mind.

choices.text: Heed Lichnowsky and bypass Belgium, sending Krupp’s mortars in first against the fortress line from Verdun to Belfort
choices.why: Take the harder road if that keeps Britain out
choices.after: Moltke objected that the plan had never foreseen such an attack. Before the French fortress line linking Verdun, Toul, Épinal and Belfort, the advance will slow.

note.text: The attack on Liège began on 5 August. Two of Krupp’s 42-centimeter mortars, still prototypes, shelled the forts from 12 August, and the last fort surrendered on 16 August. The soldiers named the gun "Big Bertha" after the Krupp heiress.

map.caption: The road through Belgium, and the French border fortress line linking Verdun, Toul and Belfort

DE-10.title: A Scrap of Paper
DE-10.clock: About five hours until Britain’s ultimatum expires (midnight, Berlin time)

telegram.text: Assurance respecting Belgian neutrality required by 12 o’clock tonight / If not, His Majesty’s Government feel bound to take all steps in their power to uphold the neutrality of Belgium / You are instructed to ask for your passports

DE-10.event: At 1 p.m. today, at the opening ceremony in the White Hall of the palace, you read the speech from the throne and then repeated what you had said from the palace balcony on 1 August: "I know no more of parties; I know only Germans!" The Social Democratic deputies stayed away from the ceremony at the palace, but at the afternoon sitting in the Reichstag building a bill for 5 billion marks in war credits passed unanimously.
DE-10.scene: The British ambassador, Goschen, having delivered the ultimatum at the Foreign Office, has come on to the Chancellor’s residence. This afternoon Bethmann Hollweg admitted in the Reichstag that the invasion of Belgium was contrary to international law. German troops across the Belgian border are heading for Liège, and Britain demands an answer by midnight.

voices.text: Your Excellency, as a signatory of the treaty on Belgian neutrality, Britain must keep its word. If it broke that word, no document Britain signed in future could be trusted.

Just for a word—"neutrality," a word which in war time had so often been disregarded—just for a scrap of paper, Great Britain was going to make war on a kindred nation who desired nothing better than to be friends with her.

voices.who: Bethmann Hollweg (Chancellor), in the Reichstag that afternoon
voices.text: Gentlemen, we are now in a state of self-defense, and necessity knows no law (Not kennt kein Gebot)!

choices.text: Heed Lichnowsky’s warning that Britain must be kept out at all costs: withdraw from Belgium and turn toward the French border
choices.why: War with Britain must be avoided, even at the cost of the war plan
choices.after: Moltke despaired that the war plan was in ruins, and the generals and the right-wing press attacked the Emperor fiercely. But the interventionists in the British cabinet lost their case for war, and London held back its declaration.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s line that necessity knows no law: reject Britain’s demand and press on through Belgium toward Liège
choices.why: Stop an advance already under way and the western campaign collapses
choices.after: The deadline passed at midnight, Berlin time, and Britain declared war on Germany. On 5 August General Leman, commander of the Liège forts, is said to have answered the demand for surrender with "Force your way through." All of Europe’s great powers but Italy, five in all, were now at war.

note.text: The British government published Goschen’s report, and "a scrap of paper" became a slogan on British recruiting posters. In his 1919 memoirs Bethmann Hollweg conceded that the expression "was perhaps an indiscretion," but explained that it had burst out of him in anger at Goschen’s harping on Belgian neutrality.

DE-10B.title: The Channel

telegram.text: British cabinet decision / If German Fleet comes into the Channel or through the North Sea to undertake hostile operations against French coasts or shipping, British Fleet will give all the protection in its power / Subject to support of Parliament

DE-10B.scene: With German troops kept out of Belgium, the Liberal cabinet in London is split down the middle over whether to go to war. The only promise Britain has made to France is to stop the German fleet if it attacks the Channel and the north coast of France. Since the naval talks with Britain in 1912, the main French fleet has been concentrated in the Mediterranean, so France’s northern coast depends in practice on the protection of the British fleet. At Wilhelmshaven, the High Seas Fleet awaits orders to sail.

voices.text: Your Majesty, you must not throw away, of your own accord, the means of putting pressure on France at sea. If Britain means to join the war anyway, a promise like this only costs Germany.

Your Majesty, if we promise to leave the Channel and France’s northern coast alone, the noninterventionists in the British cabinet will have grounds to hold out. Keep Britain on its own side of the water, and Germany can manage the war on the Continent.

choices.text: Help the noninterventionists in London hold out: promise that the German fleet will not attack the Channel or France’s north coast
choices.why: A small concession at sea may keep Britain across the water
choices.realNote: Germany did let London know that if Britain stayed neutral, the German fleet would not attack the northern coast of France. Grey, who heard of the offer just before he spoke, mentioned it in his speech to the Commons on 3 August and dismissed it: "it is far too narrow an engagement for us." Besides, in 1914 the invasion of Belgium robbed the pledge of any meaning.
choices.after: Grey informed the Commons of the pledge, and the noninterventionists in the cabinet breathed again. Britain decided to watch the war on the Continent from across the Channel.

choices.text: Follow Tirpitz: promise nothing, and keep the High Seas Fleet free to put pressure on France at sea as well
choices.why: If Britain is coming in anyway, a concession is pure loss
choices.after: In London the interventionists raised their voices, pointing to the threat of the German fleet. Britain has not yet declared war, but the Royal Navy is already guarding the North Sea on a war footing.

note.text: On 26 July, after a test mobilization, the Admiralty stopped the fleet from dispersing (the decision of the First Sea Lord, Prince Louis of Battenberg, while the First Lord, Churchill, was away). Churchill then had the main First Fleet sail from Portland on 29 July; that night it passed through the Strait of Dover with its lights out, bound for Scapa Flow in the north of Scotland.

DE-09E.place: Berlin Palace; news from the East Prussian border
DE-09E.title: A War in the East Alone

telegram.text: French mobilization complete / Troops held 10 kilometers back from frontier / No crossing

DE-09E.scene: While the German army heads east, France has completed its mobilization but watches without crossing the border. Under the alliance treaty France must fight if Germany attacks Russia, but politicians in Paris hesitate to plunge into a war in which Germany has not struck first in the west. Britain signals that it will not enter the war unless Germany attacks in the west. On the borders of East Prussia and Poland, the first clashes with the Russian army have begun.

voices.text: Your Majesty, the French army has finished mobilizing and could march into Lorraine at any time. If we seek a promise from France while leaving the west empty, Germany loses the initiative on both fronts.
Your Majesty, a nonaggression agreement with France would confine this war to the east. Neither Britain nor France would have a reason to fight, and Germany would face Russia alone.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s advice: propose mutual nonaggression to France, leaving Alsace-Lorraine to talks after the war
choices.why: Confining the war to the east is the greatest gain of all
choices.after: After long hesitation Paris agreed to talk. French nationalists were outraged at the idea of leaving Alsace-Lorraine to postwar negotiation, but the French government did not cross the border.

choices.text: Heed Moltke’s warning: do not negotiate with France, stand on the defensive in the west and throw everything into the east
choices.why: The initiative in the west is not to be bargained away
choices.after: The French army faced Germany’s fortress line across the border but did not cross first. Germany left only a minimum of troops in the west and threw all its strength into the east.

note.text: In 1914 Germany in fact placed seven armies in the west and only one, the Eighth, in East Prussia. It was that Eighth Army that destroyed the Russian Second Army at Tannenberg at the end of August.

LE-01.title: Moltke Argues for Preventive Mobilization
LE-01.clock: Third day of Russia’s partial mobilization

telegram.text: Russia keeps partial mobilization / No general mobilization proclaimed / Sazonov ready for direct talks with Vienna

LE-01.scene: Russia has stopped at partial mobilization, and the Austrian army has occupied Belgrade and gone no further. But Moltke insists that even Russia’s partial mobilization threatens Germany and demands a preventive mobilization. He is convinced that once Russia completes its rearmament in 1917, Germany will never be able to win. Peace seems within reach, yet the General Staff grows more anxious with every day’s delay.

voices.text: Your Majesty, even a partial mobilization means hundreds of thousands of troops massing on the frontier. Every day we wait puts East Prussia at greater risk, and the timetable of our war plan falls apart.

Your Majesty, if Germany mobilizes first, Russia will answer at once with general mobilization, and the blame for the war will fall on Germany. The only war the Social Democrats' workers will follow is a defensive one.

choices.text: Follow the Chancellor: do not mobilize while Russia holds at partial mobilization, and keep the high ground of defense
choices.why: Whoever moves first will bear the blame for the war
choices.after: Moltke withdrew, his face set. In St Petersburg, Sazonov breathed more easily on learning that Germany was not moving.

choices.text: Do as Moltke demands: proclaim the "state of imminent danger of war" and begin mobilization measures to defend East Prussia
choices.why: Even while the other side pauses, the mobilization timetable must hold
choices.after: Hearing that Germany had moved, the Russian General Staff talked the Tsar into general mobilization. From here the crisis followed its actual course.

note.text: The Russian General Staff had no separate plan for a partial mobilization aimed at Austria alone. That is why Russia’s generals feared that a prolonged partial mobilization would throw the whole general mobilization system into confusion.

LE-02.place: Berlin; reports from the ambassadors' conference in London
LE-02.title: What to Do with Serbia

telegram.text: Four-power ambassadors' conference opens / Austria insists on holding Belgrade until guarantees fulfilled / Russia demands immediate withdrawal

LE-02.scene: The ambassadors of the great powers sit down together again at the Foreign Office in London. Austria says it will occupy Belgrade until Serbia keeps its promises; Russia demands immediate withdrawal. Where the conference goes depends on which side Germany takes, and you must decide whether to put your ally’s pride or Russia’s patience first.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Vienna believes that only by holding Belgrade can it make Serbia keep its promises. If Germany tells it to pull back now, Austria will have been humiliated twice over.
Your Majesty, Russia demands withdrawal for the sake of its prestige. Give Russia a way out it can accept, such as an international commission of observers, and the conference will succeed.

choices.text: Side with Tschirschky: back Austria to the end in its demand to hold Belgrade until Serbia has kept every promise
choices.why: An ally must not be left to suffer a second humiliation
choices.after: Vienna was overjoyed, but anger in St Petersburg deepened. The Russian papers wrote that the Slav brothers had been abandoned once again.

choices.text: Put forward Lichnowsky’s plan: an international commission to supervise Serbia’s inquiry, and Austrian troops withdrawn
choices.why: The conference can succeed only if Russia too has a way out
choices.after: The conference accepted the mediation plan. Vienna swallowed its displeasure, and newspapers in London and Paris hailed the German Emperor as a peacemaker.

choices.text: Go to Russia directly, as Bismarck did with the Reinsurance Treaty, and propose a secret pact dividing the Balkans into spheres
choices.why: A deal with Russia that bypasses Vienna is the surer course
choices.after: Sazonov showed interest, but Vienna was enraged by rumors that Germany had dealt behind its back, and trust within the alliance was badly shaken.

note.text: The London Conference of Ambassadors in 1913 blocked Serbia’s hoped-for outlet to the Adriatic and made Albania independent. The decision left deep resentment in Serbia.

LE-03.title: The Charge of Humiliation
LE-03.scene: The Pan-German League, the army and the conservative press accuse the Emperor of backing down before Russia. The Social Democrats, who won 110 seats in the 1912 election and became the largest party in the Reichstag, support the decision that kept the peace. The army demands that it be enlarged further before Russia’s rearmament is complete, and the next general election is due in 1917.

voices.who: Heinrich Class (chairman of the Pan-German League)
voices.text: Your Majesty’s retreat before Russia is a disgrace to Germany. As in Morocco in 1911, Germany has once again half drawn the sword and then put it back.

voices.who: Hugo Haase (co-chairman of the Social Democratic Party)
voices.text: Germany’s workers did not want to shed their blood over the Balkans. The Social Democrats support the decision that kept the peace. But if more armaments are to be the price of it, we will oppose them.

choices.text: Placate the army and the conservatives: put a new army bill to the Reichstag, building on the Army Law of 1913
choices.why: Only a bigger army will quiet the critics at home
choices.after: The army and the conservatives were mollified, and the new budget passed the Reichstag with the votes of the Center Party and the conservatives. But St Petersburg and Paris raised their own budgets again in answer to Germany’s buildup.

choices.text: Hold Moltke responsible for endangering the peace, remove him as chief of staff, and keep the army out of diplomacy
choices.why: Diplomacy belongs to the Emperor and the Chancellor, not the army
choices.after: The General Staff was stunned and the conservative press attacked the Emperor. But Europe’s capitals watched the change in Berlin with relief.

note.text: In 1913 the Social Democrats did in fact oppose the army increase while voting for the one-time defense levy on property that paid for it. The Army Law passed on 3 July 1913 raised the peacetime strength in rank and file by about 117,000, bringing the total, officers and NCOs included, to about 800,000.

PE-00.title: After the Refusal
PE-00.scene: Vienna’s Foreign Ministry is stunned by the news that Germany has refused unconditional support. Even so, Franz Joseph’s court is determined that those behind the Archduke’s murderers shall not go unpunished, and it is preparing demands on Serbia. You must leave soon on your Norwegian cruise, and before you go you have to decide how Europe is to see this refusal. War Minister Falkenhayn has sent word that the army cannot accept the decision.

voices.text: Your Majesty, if Austria is made to back down once again, Germany will stand alone in the middle of Europe against Russia and France. Many officers think that now, before Russia has finished its preparations, is the better moment.
Your Majesty, there is no need to make the refusal known. Quietly give Vienna time to step back with its dignity intact, and meanwhile ask Russia to calm Serbia down.

choices.text: Telegraph Nicky and ask Russia to prevail on Belgrade so that Serbia cooperates with the inquiry into the assassination
choices.why: With Russia on board, Vienna and Belgrade can both step back
choices.after: Nicholas II sent a warm reply condemning the crime, and Sazonov advised Belgrade to act with caution. Vienna was hurt that the German Emperor had spoken to the Tsar before speaking to Austria.

choices.text: Follow the Chancellor: keep the refusal secret and quietly give Vienna time to step back with its dignity intact
choices.why: An alliance lasts only if the ally’s dignity is protected
choices.after: The official statements from Berlin and Vienna spoke only of the firm solidarity of the two allies. But inside Vienna’s Foreign Ministry the story quietly spread that Germany had turned its back at the decisive moment.

choices.text: Call in the Reichstag party leaders and make it plain that Germany will not go to war over a Balkan quarrel
choices.why: A decision made public is one the army cannot overturn
choices.after: The Social Democrats and the Progressive People’s Party welcomed the Emperor’s decision, while the conservative press accused him of backing down as in the Moroccan crisis of 1911. Once Germany’s refusal was public, Vienna felt deeply humiliated.

note.text: In fact, the Chancellor and the military chiefs who met at the New Palace on the afternoon of 5 July judged that the sooner Austria moved the better, and that Russia, though Serbia’s friend, would in the end stay out. Moltke, the chief of the General Staff, was not present.

PE-01.title: Austria Without Germany

telegram.text: Austria delivers softened note / Serbia replies it will cooperate with international inquiry / Talk of "German betrayal" in Viennese political circles

PE-01.scene: Without German backing, Austria sent Serbia a softened note, and Serbia replied that it would cooperate with an international inquiry. The crisis has subsided, but in Vienna people say openly that Germany has abandoned the alliance. Tisza, the Hungarian prime minister, is relieved, but Conrad and the younger diplomats resent Berlin. Germany’s bond with the only ally it can rely on is fraying.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Vienna believes Germany turned its back at the decisive moment. If this wound is left to fester, Austria will one day look for another path.
Your Majesty, a wound to the alliance can be healed with money and time, but a war with Russia cannot be undone. Germany should seize this chance to become the mediator between Russia and Austria.

choices.text: Heed Tschirschky’s warning and soothe Vienna’s hurt with the promise of a loan and arms, Krupp guns among them
choices.why: Only practical help will heal the alliance’s wound
choices.after: Vienna accepted the German loan, but the resentment did not easily fade. St Petersburg grew wary that Germany was rearming Austria.

choices.text: Mediate the Balkan negotiations between Russia and Austria yourself, as Bismarck did at the Congress of Berlin in 1878
choices.why: As mediator Germany can guard both its prestige and its safety
choices.after: The Russian and Austrian ambassadors sat down together in Berlin. The role of "honest broker" that Bismarck had claimed at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 fell to Germany once more.

choices.text: Let Vienna nurse its resentment, since Austria has no one but Germany to lean on, and keep the alliance to the bare minimum
choices.why: Vienna has nowhere else to go, so there is no need to soothe it
choices.after: Relations between Vienna and Berlin grew cool. Vienna’s diplomats quietly began to weigh other options.

note.text: In fact, at the Austro-Hungarian joint council of ministers on 7 July 1914, Tisza alone opposed a surprise attack on Serbia. Under the Dual Monarchy it was hard to decide on war without the consent of the Hungarian prime minister.

PE-02.title: Moltke’s Case for a Preventive War
PE-02.scene: Moltke argues that once Russia’s "Great Programme," enacted in the summer of 1914, is completed in 1917, Germany will never be able to win, so it must fight before then. He said the same at the meeting of military chiefs you called in December 1912. The General Staff’s maps show the new strategic railways being laid in western Russia with French loans.

voices.who: Moltke (chief of the General Staff), at the meeting of military chiefs on 8 December 1912 (from Admiral von Müller’s diary)
voices.text: I consider a war inevitable—the sooner, the better.

Your Majesty, rattling the saber in every diplomatic quarrel where neither Germany’s honor nor its security nor its future is at stake is reckless. War is a course Germany may choose only when its very existence is at stake.

choices.text: Take the Chancellor’s view: reject preventive war and make it clear to the General Staff that Germany will not start a war
choices.why: Only a threat to the nation’s existence can justify starting a war
