choices.after: Moltke was disappointed, and there was muttering at the General Staff that the Emperor had gone soft. But Europe’s capitals took note of Berlin’s restraint.

choices.text: Reject preventive war, but answer Russia’s rearmament with a new army bill, as in 1913
choices.why: The balance of power must be kept, even without war
choices.after: A new army bill went to the Reichstag. Paris and St Petersburg promptly answered in kind, and the arms race climbed another step.

choices.text: Accept Moltke’s logic and agree with the General Staff that in the next crisis Germany will fight before Russia is ready
choices.why: Every year that passes only makes Russia stronger
choices.after: Moltke was satisfied. The General Staff went on refining the western war plan year after year.

note.text: The meeting of military chiefs on 8 December 1912 was held without Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg, and historians disagree over whether it should be seen as a "war council" that resolved on war. Moltke’s words survive in the diary of Admiral von Müller, chief of the Naval Cabinet.

PE-03.title: A Chance to End the Naval Race
PE-03.scene: Britain proposes fresh talks on scaling back the naval race. When the British war secretary, Haldane, came to Berlin in 1912, Germany demanded a British promise of neutrality in return for slowing its fleet building, and the talks failed. The High Seas Fleet, built up under Tirpitz’s Navy Laws, is a symbol of German prestige, but it also drove Britain toward France and Russia. Since the widening of the Kiel Canal in June 1914, even dreadnoughts can pass between the North Sea and the Baltic.

voices.text: Your Majesty, the fleet is a risk fleet that keeps Britain from treating Germany lightly. Slow its growth, and far from being grateful, Britain will remember only Germany’s weakness.
Your Majesty, a naval agreement with Britain is the surest way to separate Britain from France and Russia. A few battleships are not worth more than a friendly power.

choices.text: Follow the Chancellor: slow the pace of fleet building, and in return ask Britain for a promise of neutrality, as in 1912
choices.why: Britain’s neutrality is worth more than a few battleships
choices.after: London balked at a neutrality pledge, but the talks went on. Tirpitz hinted at resignation, and the Navy League accused the Emperor of giving up the sea.

choices.text: Follow Tirpitz: reject Britain’s proposal and carry on building battleships as the Navy Laws require
choices.why: Only a strong fleet will win Britain’s respect
choices.after: The talks broke down again. The British Admiralty put a new battleship budget before Parliament.

note.text: After Haldane went home empty-handed in February 1912, Germany passed an amended Navy Law, and Britain, reducing its Mediterranean fleet to concentrate in the North Sea, reached naval arrangements with France.

PE-03B.place: Berlin, the Prussian Diet and the Reichstag
PE-03B.title: A Red Reichstag and the Three-Class Franchise
PE-03B.clock: About a year until the Reichstag election (January 1917)
PE-03B.scene: As the peace lengthens, domestic questions return. The Reichstag is elected by universal male suffrage, but the Diet of Prussia, home to three-fifths of Germany’s population, is elected under the three-class franchise, which gives more weight to the votes of those who pay the most tax. The Social Democrats demand that the system be changed and aim for an even bigger victory in the 1917 election. Some conservatives even talk recklessly of dissolving the Reichstag and changing the electoral law.

voices.who: Ernst von Heydebrand (leader of the Prussian Conservatives)
voices.text: Your Majesty, the three-class franchise is a pillar of the Prussian monarchy. Yield one step to the Social Democrats, and next they will demand the crown.

Your Majesty, my franchise reform bill of 1910 collapsed under conservative opposition. But as long as the workers are kept outside the state, the Empire will be shaken from within. Careful reform is the way to prevent revolution.

choices.text: Revive the Chancellor’s 1910 bill to reform Prussia’s three-class franchise, and compromise with moderate Social Democrats
choices.why: Timely reform is the way to head off revolution
choices.after: The conservatives protested furiously, but the reform moved forward little by little. Within the Social Democratic Party, the moderates who favored compromise with the Emperor grew louder.

choices.text: Follow Heydebrand: refuse reform and rely on the army and the conservatives to preserve the order of the Prussian monarchy
choices.why: Yield one step and the whole monarchy will totter
choices.after: Franchise demonstrations continued in the streets, and the Social Democrats set their sights on the next election. The army began to speak of "the enemy within."

choices.text: Instead of reform, turn the nation’s eyes abroad with a new fleet program and a plan for colonies in Central Africa
choices.why: Prestige won abroad will cover discontent at home
choices.after: The new fleet program and the African colonial plan filled the front pages. Discontent at home subsided for a while, but London and Paris watched warily for Germany’s next move.

note.text: Historians such as Hans-Ulrich Wehler put forward the "social imperialism" interpretation, which holds that Germany’s ruling elites used overseas expansion and naval policy to deflect demands for reform at home, but the interpretation has many critics.

PE-04.title: The Old Emperor Dies

telegram.text: Emperor Franz Joseph dead at Schönbrunn Palace / Reigned 68 years / Archduke Karl succeeds

PE-04.scene: Emperor Franz Joseph, who ruled the multinational empire for 68 years, has died at 86. The new emperor, Karl, is 29. In Hungary, the Czech lands and the South Slav regions, calls for self-rule grow louder, and in the streets of Vienna people ask whether the empire can survive without the old Emperor.

voices.text: Your Majesty, all this talk of federalism or a triple monarchy means tearing the Kingdom of Hungary apart. Hungary cannot give up a single letter of the Compromise of 1867.

voices.who: Karl I (the new emperor of Austria-Hungary)
voices.text: Your Majesty, unless the peoples of the empire are given more self-rule, they will look for their future outside it. Reform needs Germany’s support.

choices.text: Side with Tisza and promise Vienna that Germany will prevent the breakup of the Dual Monarchy, by sending troops if need be
choices.why: If the ally collapses, Germany too will stand alone
choices.after: Vienna’s conservatives were relieved. But Czech and South Slav nationalists, fearing that German troops might come, began to look toward Russia and Serbia.

choices.text: Back Emperor Karl’s federal reform and promise loans and economic aid to support it
choices.why: Without reform the ally will not last long
choices.after: With Germany’s backing Karl put forward his reform plan, but Budapest’s resistance was fierce. Slowly, the empire began to change.

choices.text: Stay out of the Habsburg empire’s internal affairs and leave reform or the status quo to Vienna and Budapest
choices.why: Germany must not be dragged into another state’s domestic quarrels
choices.after: Vienna felt that Germany had turned its back once again. The Triple Alliance survived only on paper, and Berlin stood more and more alone in the middle of Europe.

note.text: Franz Joseph did in fact die at Schönbrunn Palace on 21 November 1916, and his successor, Karl I, would witness the breakup of the empire two years later.

PE-05.title: The Balkan Crisis Returns
PE-05.clock: The year Russia’s "Great Programme" is completed

telegram.text: Clashes on Balkan frontier / Russian military districts preparing to mobilize / Vienna asks Germany’s position

PE-05.scene: Crisis has broken out in the Balkans again. Russia has completed its rearmament under the "Great Programme" and finished the strategic railways to its western border. The chief of the General Staff says this is the last chance; the Chancellor urges a conference, as in 1914. Now it will be seen whether the peace you kept in the summer of 1914 merely bought time or opened a different road.

voices.who: Chief of the General Staff (Moltke’s successor)
voices.text: Your Majesty, Russia is ready. If we do not move today, Germany will only fall further behind each year. This is the last chance.
Your Majesty, we heard the same words in 1914. A conference kept the peace then, and it can keep it now.

choices.text: Follow the Chancellor: propose an ambassadors' conference of the powers, as in 1914, with Germany mediating in person
choices.why: What kept the peace once may keep it again
choices.after: At Berlin’s proposal the ambassadors of the powers gathered once more. But the outcome will turn on three years of accumulated armaments and mistrust.

choices.text: Follow the chief of staff: order mobilization, seizing 1917 as the last chance before Russia grows any stronger
choices.why: Wait any longer and Germany can never win
choices.after: With the mobilization order, Europe’s railways filled again with troop trains. The great war, arriving three years late, will be fought with more men and heavier guns.

note.text: In 1917 the Russian Empire in fact collapsed in the revolution of March (February, Old Style). Without a war, there is no knowing which way Russia’s rearmament and its internal crisis would have tipped.

epilogues.A: When the summer of 1914 passed without war, the Pan-German League sneered at you as the "Peace Emperor," but Germany’s factories and shipyards never stopped, and the empire went on growing as one of Europe’s greatest industrial powers. Yet 1917, the year Moltke had warned of, when Russia’s rearmament would be complete, was still drawing nearer, and the alliance system and the arms race remained as they were. The real Wilhelm II lost his throne and went into exile in the Netherlands in November 1918, and he died at Doorn on 4 June 1941 without ever setting foot on German soil again.
epilogues.B: The Austrian army stayed in Belgrade, and you made your name as the mediator who stopped a war between Vienna and St Petersburg. But in Russia, which had already backed down before Germany and Austria in the Bosnian crisis of 1909, the humiliation festered, and Russia’s generals vowed never to back down again. In reality, the Austrian army took Belgrade only on 2 December 1914, and lost it to the Serbian army again two weeks later.
epilogues.C: The German army fought the Russians on the plains of Poland, and no trenches appeared on the western frontier. Alsace-Lorraine remained German, but the French army stood waiting across the border with its guns trained on Germany, and no one can say whether a war in the east alone would have brought down the Tsarist regime sooner or tied Germany down longer. In reality, the German army destroyed the Russian Second Army at Tannenberg at the end of August, but in the west its advance was halted on the Marne in September.
epilogues.D: With no British fleet blockading the North Sea, Germany’s ports stayed open, and the food shortages that in reality brought on the "turnip winter" of 1916–1917 would have been far less severe. Germany fought France and Russia; it might, as the historian Niall Ferguson has argued, have won quickly and come to dominate the Continent, or France and Russia might have held out longer even without Britain. You would be remembered as the emperor who kept Britain out, but Britain would never have welcomed a continent ruled by a single power.
epilogues.E: Moltke stepped down after the defeat on the Marne in September 1914 and died in 1916. Bethmann Hollweg lost his eldest son on the Eastern Front in December 1914 and was forced out of the chancellorship by the military in July 1917. From August 1916, when the Supreme Army Command of Hindenburg and Ludendorff took real power, you were pushed aside as a "shadow emperor," and amid defeat and revolution in November 1918 you fled to the Netherlands, signing your abdication at Amerongen on 28 November. Article 227 of the Treaty of Versailles called for you to be put on trial before an international tribunal, but the Netherlands refused to hand you over, and you died at Doorn in 1941. Some two million German soldiers died in the war.
epilogues.F: The peace of the summer of 1914 ended three years later. The great war that came once Russia’s Great Programme and Germany’s army expansion were both complete was fought with more men and heavier guns, and once again Germany had to fight in the west and the east at the same time. The peace you kept in 1914 only bought time, and you will be remembered as the emperor who ordered mobilization in 1917.

dossier.t: Born in 1859 and on the throne since 1888, he is 55 in July 1914. A grandson of Britain’s Queen Victoria, he had a troubled relationship with his mother, Victoria, a British princess. His left arm, injured at birth, was of little use to him. He speaks impulsively and theatrically, and likes to scrawl notes peppered with exclamation marks in the margins of reports. Together with his navy secretary, Tirpitz, he threw himself into building a great battle fleet.

Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg, a careful bureaucrat, had sunk into deep pessimism after losing his wife in May 1914. Moltke, chief of the General Staff, had said at a meeting in December 1912 that war was unavoidable and the sooner the better, and in the spring of 1914 he still believed Germany must fight before Russia grew stronger. Jagow, state secretary at the Foreign Office, and Tirpitz, the navy secretary, also pressed their views on the Emperor. What the Emperor learned, and when, lay largely in these men’s hands.

His greatest fear was Russia. The belief had spread through the leadership, above all the military, that once Russia’s huge rearmament program was finished around 1917, Germany could no longer win. There was also a strong sense of being encircled by Britain, France and Russia. At home, the Social Democrats had become the largest party in the Reichstag in the 1912 election. His hope was that the war would stay between Austria and Serbia, and that Britain, where his cousin George V was king, would stay neutral.

movers.intro: How much responsibility Wilhelm II bears for the war is a question historians have long debated. The main views are these:
views: John Röhl: sees the Emperor’s "personal rule" and the politics of his entourage as central to German policy. He argues that at the meeting of December 1912 Germany’s leaders decided to put off war for about a year and a half and prepare for it, and that in the July crisis, too, the Emperor was a central figure steering toward war.

Christopher Clark: holds that the Emperor was crude in speech and erratic, but that at the decisive moments of the July crisis he was sidelined by the Chancellor and the military, and his real influence was limited. Rather than pinning the war on one country, he explains it as the result of misjudgments by leaders in many countries.

Annika Mombauer: stresses the military’s pressure for preventive war, led by Moltke, and the rigidity of a single war plan, and places the main responsibility for the war on the leaderships of Germany and Austria-Hungary.

Fritz Fischer: argued in a 1961 book that Germany’s leaders, aiming at hegemony in Europe and world-power status, deliberately accepted the risk of a great war, and in a 1969 book went so far as to say they had been preparing for war since around the meeting of December 1912. His thesis set off a major controversy in West Germany in the 1960s.
movers.note: Röhl and others give weight to the effect of the Emperor’s withered left arm and his relationship with his mother on his character, but many object that this reads too much into them.
